name: Anti-looksmax / 'touch grass' critiques

lead: This entry covers criticism of looksmaxxing, from academic and press critiques to the casual 'touch grass' jab.
Critics cite anecdote-based claims, injury risks and ties to incel ideology, while practitioners may see the criticism differently.

paras: Critique appears in journalism, academic papers and online replies telling heavy users to go outside.
No direct risks; the topic concerns reported harms such as body dysmorphia and injuries from practices like bonesmashing.

lead: Critiques of looksmaxxing come from journalists, researchers, clinicians and others who argue the practice is harmful or misguided; a common informal version tells practitioners to 'touch grass', a phrase meaning go outside, used mockingly at people who seem absorbed in online content.[1]

Wikipedia's looksmaxxing article records several lines of criticism: that the movement is judgmental, that mewing and 'bonesmashing' are regarded as misinformation by doctors and researchers, that it relies on anecdote and promotes male supremacy, and that it may channel young men toward incel views.[2]

paras: Writer Becca Rothfeld described the moral objections as numerous in The New Yorker in 2026.[2] Researchers, including Halpin and colleagues (2025), say the practice rests on anecdotal evidence and links to hegemonic masculinity.[2]
Facial surgeons warn that bonesmashing can cause fractures and other injuries, and doctors dismiss mewing claims as misinformation.[2]
Reporting by the BBC and Guardian in 2024 linked communities that rate appearance with body dysmorphia and suicidal ideation, and users rated below average may face harassment.[2]
A glossary describes 'touch grass' as believed to have originated in 2015 and revived in 2020 to 2021, used as a light jab at people who spend too long online.[1]
